title: When discharge predictions drift
subtitle: What a five-day ICU simulator gets wrong—and why
scope: ICU care after the first 24 hours
message: A model developed on earlier ICU data systematically overpredicts later ICU discharge. Nearly all of its five-day discharge error is visible before recursively simulating future physiology. The mismatch persists after standardizing measured case mix; it cannot be attributed to a change in care policy alone.

decisions.description: Weighted differences in pre/post support and monitoring around newly documented DNR orders. Associations, not effects of a DNR intervention.
decisions.comparison: First observed DNR order versus eligible documented-full-code risk sets at the same ICU elapsed time
decisions.caution: The matched groups retain very different 12-hour mortality: 16.9% versus 1.7%. Important unmeasured prognosis or clinical intentions remain.

simulation.name: Longitudinal stochastic ICU trajectory model
simulation.caution: The model tracks observed mortality incidence relatively closely, but overestimates ICU discharge and underestimates ICU occupancy. It is not validated for decision support or counterfactual policy.

documentation.label: Undocumented structured code status at the six-hour landmark
documentation.caution: An unknown charted code status is not evidence of full-code intent. Temporal drift may reflect documentation practices.

takeaways.label: What the error decomposition reveals
takeaways.text: Approximately 6.37 of 6.69 points of excess simulated five-day ICU discharge are already present on actual patient histories.

takeaways.label: What the historical comparison adds
takeaways.text: Later ICU discharge remains about 3.41 points lower after recorded baseline common-support standardization, with important unobserved case-mix caveats.

takeaways.label: What remains unsuccessful
takeaways.text: Simulated long-horizon discharge and ICU occupancy do not pass the prespecified validity gates.

methods.cohort: One ICU stay per patient. Six-hour landmarks from ICU hour 24 through day seven.
methods.historical_split: Primary: training 2008–2016, calibration 2017–2019, later exploratory test 2020–2022. Earlier rolling-origin: training 2008–2013, calibration 2014–2016, evaluation 2017–2019.
methods.metrics: Multiclass log loss, Brier score, paired patient-clustered uncertainty, multi-horizon cumulative incidence and explicit calibration gates.
warnings: Observational single-centre data; not a randomized study.
DNR is a code-status designation, not an instruction to stop otherwise indicated treatment.
Predictive information cannot be causally attributed to treatment choices without further identifying assumptions.
The test period was revisited during iterative model development; results are exploratory, not untouched final confirmation.
Selection through ICU exit and death changes the observation process.
No patient-level data, identifiable records or clinical recommendations are published.
The 2020–2022 cohort was examined during model development; these findings are exploratory, not a fresh prospective holdout.
Patient-bootstrap uncertainty for prequential and standardized contrasts conditions on fitted model and overlap weights; simulator replicates quantify Monte Carlo uncertainty, not model uncertainty.
The residual change after measured case-mix standardization does not identify a policy effect; hidden patient severity, coding practice and discharge circumstances may differ.
The model still fails discharge and occupancy trajectory validation. It must not be used for clinical decision support.

Derived ventilation and vasopressor interval endpoints can incorporate charting recorded after the landmark. The retrospective forecasting study has not established real-time, as-of-feature availability.

transport.title: Dissecting the five-day discharge error
transport.comparison_label: 2020–2022 cohort, first ICU stay, alive at hour 24
transport.description: Prequential prediction uses the patient's ACTUAL recorded histories; recursive rollout generates its own future histories. Their difference is a diagnostic, not a causal effect or a formal variance decomposition.

historical_shift.definition: Baseline-overlap standardized cumulative ICU discharge during the five days after hour 24; cross-fitted domain propensity uses recorded baseline covariates only. Remaining shift can reflect unmeasured case mix and documentation as well as hospital practice.

scientific_limitations: The 2020–2022 cohort was examined during model development; these findings are exploratory, not a fresh prospective holdout.
Patient-bootstrap uncertainty for prequential and standardized contrasts conditions on fitted model and overlap weights; simulator replicates quantify Monte Carlo uncertainty, not model uncertainty.
The residual change after measured case-mix standardization does not identify a policy effect; hidden patient severity, coding practice and discharge circumstances may differ.
The model still fails discharge and occupancy trajectory validation. It must not be used for clinical decision support.
ICU stay end does not necessarily mean permanent ICU discharge; about 2–3% of baseline patients had a first-ICU exit followed by another ICU admission within 24 hours.

icu_return_sensitivity.method: Retrospective same-hospital-admission ICU return within 24 hours following the first ICU exit; does not reclassify the original competing endpoint for predictive modeling.
icu_return_sensitivity.caveat: Whether a first-ICU-stay exit is followed by an ICU return is only known after the event; this is an administrative endpoint sensitivity, not a prospective transition definition.
